t: Chinese folk religion has no single church or creed: one takes part by belonging to a village, a lineage or a temple association with its gods and rituals, not by believing an official doctrine.
Its common core is Tian, Heaven, the source of moral meaning; qi, the energy of which all things are made; the veneration of ancestors; and bao ying, moral reciprocity.
Condemned as “feudal superstition” after 1911 and attacked most of all in the Cultural Revolution (1966–1976), it revived after 1978, with millions of temples rebuilt or built from scratch.
dyk: Many temples in northern China reopened because their gods were said to reclaim them: a Chenghuang Temple in Yulin, Shaanxi, used as a granary in the Cultural Revolution, was restored in the 1980s after the seeds stored in it were always found to have rotted.
ev: Divination, a major component of folk religion, has developed in China by 1250–1150 BCE
The Yijing and the Eight Trigrams are well established
A cult of Ganesha, the Elephant-Head God, is attested, as influences from the Indian subcontinent arrive with the spread of Buddhism
Under the Song dynasty folk practices blend with Buddhist, Confucian and Taoist teachings into the popular religion that lasts to the present
Kang Youwei persuades the emperor to order temples that perform no state sacrifices turned into schools; the confiscations are soon reversed
The Nationalist government’s “Standards for retaining or abolishing gods and shrines” try to abolish the cults of all gods but great heroes and sages
The Cultural Revolution makes the most serious and last systematic effort to destroy the ancient Chinese religion
After the adoption of the new constitution the religion revives rapidly, with millions of temples rebuilt or built from scratch

f.origin: China, from the beginnings of Chinese civilisation: ancestor veneration from prehistory and divination by 1250–1150 BCE; as popular religion distinct from the Three Teachings, primarily from the Song dynasty (960–1279).
f.founder: none: it grew from local cults of gods, immortals and ancestors, bound to villages, lineages and temples rather than to a founder or a church.
f.scriptures: none of its own: it draws on a vast heritage of sacred books, from the Confucian classics and the I Ching to the Taoist Daodejing, the precious scrolls (baojuan) of the folk sects, morality books and works of mythology.
f.followers: Yang and Hu (2012) counted 55.5% of China’s adults, 578 million people; the China Family Panel Studies’ 2012 survey found 81% of China’s population (1 billion) worshipping gods and ancestors in the traditional way; in Taiwan 42.7% of adults (16 million) are self-identified folk believers.
